text: After this you can explain how identification, decisions, records and verification work together.

A product is more than the object in front of you. Its controlled description tells a team which components, software and instructions belong to a particular version. Configuration management keeps that description usable as work proceeds. First, identify the important parts. Then review proposed changes, record decisions and work, and compare records with the product. These jobs reinforce one another. A change log needs item identities. Even a complete parts list fails when changes bypass control.

items: Name the product and its intended version. You should see: A record distinguishes it from similar products. If not: Create a provisional identity and have the responsible owner confirm it.
List the pieces and documents requiring control. You should see: An item list links each controlled element to its description. If not: Start with safety, function and difficult-to-replace elements.
Find the approved reference state. You should see: You know the version against which changes will be judged. If not: Mark the state unknown; do not call a draft approved.
Compare the current item with the records. You should see: Differences are investigated rather than silently accepted. If not: Log unresolved differences for review.
Imagine a fictional modular product. The replaceable module may be unchanged while the control software is updated. The unit record should make both facts visible.

text: Identify, then Review changes, then Record status, then Verify
A usable configuration record identifies the item, the decision and the resulting state.
It cannot prove the real item matches without inspection or other evidence.

items: Keeping only the newest drawing A later document does not reveal which earlier units were actually upgraded. Fix: Retain version history and unit-level evidence.
